title: "First half – The claim and its reproduction"
---
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
**Slides.** [Open the deck at this half](../../slides/housing-short.html#/half-1-the-claim-and-its-reproduction){target="_blank"} in its own tab, or follow it on the [slides page](slides.qmd).
:::

The first half gives you the vocabulary of three kinds of repetition and the case, an experiment run by email, and works out what question its claim answers. Before the break you reproduce the result that one of the five independent analysts of the claim reported, whichever of them you choose, and find out why your number is exactly that number.

| Work through | What you do | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Slides, the opening | The plan of the session, and what you do not need: nothing to install, no git, and no GitHub or OSF account. Open the [browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd) in a tab while the facilitator talks. | 3 minutes |
| Slides, the first half | The matrix of data against analysis that separates reproducibility, robustness and replicability; the SCORE programme in brief; and Multi100 from the inside: what an analyst received, the two tasks, and how the results were put on a common scale. | 12 minutes |
| [Browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-1-setup) Task 1 | The setup check. Wait for the R engine, run the setup cell, and check that `audit` has 1,014 rows and that the last line reports −19.97 percentage points. The warm-up on the three Rs gives you something to do while the engine downloads. | 5 minutes |
| Slides, the paper and the five analysts | The paper of the original authors (OAs): the question that it asks, the design, the email word for word, what came back for each of the six names, the four outcomes that were coded, and the claim as SCORE selected it. Then the five Multi100 analysts, with five different questions behind two different verdicts. | 18 minutes |
| Slides, the estimand and the graph | The estimand statement, which everyone writes in chat, holds and sends together; the causal graph of the experiment; why comparing greetings among the replies conditions on a consequence of the name; and what changes when every delivered email is counted. | 12 minutes |
| Slides, the reproduction | The instruction of Task 2 of Multi100 read word for word, what it left open, and the aim of the reproduction: one of the five reanalyses, whichever you choose, from the public file of the OAs. | 6 minutes |
| [Browser lab](../../cases/housing/lab.qmd#task-3-reproduction) Task 3 | Choose one of the five analysts and complete their cell on the public file `audit_original.csv`. Four of them have a value that Multi100 recorded: $\chi^2$ = 14.265 for 8PTRZ, z = −3.771 for UYV3F, z = 3.645 for EWFMI and $\chi^2$ = 13.683 for 25N5D. P9W8Y has none, so its test of three groups, $\chi^2$ = 15.951 on 2 degrees of freedom, can be run again but not matched. Everyone types the analyst and the value without sending them, and sends them when the facilitator says go. | 14 minutes |
| Slides | The continuity correction, which `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` apply to a two-by-two table unless they are told otherwise, so that `correct = FALSE` gives 14.95 for 8PTRZ and 14.33 for 25N5D; the base group that sets the sign of the z of EWFMI; and why everyone who chose the same analyst got the same value while the five analysts, each writing their own code, did not. | 5 minutes |

**By the end of the half** you have written the estimand statement behind the claim, you know why comparing among the replies and counting every delivered email answer two different questions, and you have reproduced one of the five reanalyses yourself and know on which defaults of the software its value depends.
